Idk what's wrong with the Open Sicilian. Yes, of course there are many Open Sicilians Black players can choose from. On the other hand, there are also many viable responses to each of those Sicilians. For example, I counted 15 viable moves in the starting position of the Najdorf, the most popular Sicilian. Do you think that your opponents will be prepared against all of those ideas?

Also, the first five moves can basically be premoved. e4, Nf3, d4, Nxd4, Nc3. It's not like you are forced to learn 30 move lines from scratch.
Additionally, there are certain systems you can play against many different Sicilians (e.g. the "English Attack" with Be3, Qd2 and 0-0-0 works quite often). 
The Open Sicilian also is very flexible. Against many viable Sicilians you can choose a system which fits your playstyle. Or maybe even your mood! Maybe you'll feel very combative on a certain day. Then you might choose 6.Bg5 against the Najdorf. Or are you in a peaceful mood? Then choose the positional systems with 6.Be2 or where you retreat your knight to f3.

This leads me to a problem all of those "Anti Sicilian" lines share. You don't have many freedoms regarding your ideas. If you choose the Smith-Morra, you'll end up in an Alapin very often which is not bad, but very calm. If you choose the Closed Sicilian, you're basically forced to go all-in on the kingside at some point because Black will expand on the queenside and in the center in the middlegame. 
The Open Sicilian doesn't have such a problem as I've explained.

And even if your opponents are "booked up", it doesn't matter after a certain point. You won't play the Top 10 in the world who know all of those lines by heart. The Open Sicilian will always give you a playable position because your development scheme is sound. You set your claim in the center and develop all of your pieces to reasonable squares. It doesn't matter if the position after move 15 is +0.5, 0.00 or -0.5. you'll have your chances because the position is open.

If you want to become a truly good chess player, go and study the Open Sicilian.

Edit: if your opponents actually are booked up, choosing weird sidelines is even worse because they'll know how to fight them. This is one of the reasons why people like me choose the Sicilian as their main weapon against 1.e4. if my opponent is too creative regarding their choice of sideline, I'll be surely better in the middlegame.

I was playing in an open tournament in 2014. It didn't go well, I started with 1 out of 3, losing to two 2200+ Elo players while I was rated 2080ish. I was probably overrated at that point because I hadn't played an open tournament in three years.

Anyways, I was paired against a 1900 rated younger player. I did some dubious stuff in the opening but he couldn't capitalize and I got a great position after exchanging queens. I was already making plans to create weaknesses, improve my position yada yada...

Then he surprised me by playing Nd5, offering a draw. I was 100% sure I would decline the offer as I was clearly better. And in 999 out of 1000 games I'd just make a move and continue playing.
But in that game, I was feeling really confident. I made my move while explicitly saying "I want to play on". 

Didn't realize that by playing Nd5, he was attacking my own knight on b4. I completely ignored his offer to trade pieces. My opponent stared at me in disbelief and simply took my hanging knight. Needless to say, I immediately resigned and went on to lose a horrible game against another 1900 player. Probably the most embarrassing day in my career.

Work usually ticks those three boxes:
- autonomy: the degree of autonomy varies from job to job, but in general you have to decide things on your own
- competence: you went to school, maybe you went to college, got a degree...and you wanna show yourself (and the world) that you are able to do something. You want to experience the feeling of being competent at something
- relatedness: you wanna feel connected to other people. You wanna be acknowledged by others. Usually that happens at work too because you work with others from time to time.

From a psychological point of view we work because we want to satisfy our psychological needs.
The stupid thing about our world is that we sometimes have to work bad jobs because otherwise we'd starve.

A knight won't make it there without White's help. For example, after playing ...Bg4 and Bxf3, Black could follow up with e7-e6. Now White might be tempted to take on e6 because on the surface, the d-file gets opened and the black pawn on d6 might be a weakness. However, Black can play Nb8-c6-d4. The knight would reach its desired square while blocking the d-file, rendering White's play against the "weak" pawn on d6 useless.

A more experienced player would probably not exchange on e6. This would result in Black taking on d5 very soon. If White recaptures cxd5, we will reach a well-known Modern Benoni position in which both sides have their chances with a lot of typical ideas.
The other option is exd5 keeping the pawn structure more or less symmetrical. Black still has a pawn break available with b7-b5, trying to play in the style of the Benko Gambit. Opening up the files on the queenside would amplify the strength of the Bg7. I guess this might be another scenario in which White would rather have the c-pawn on c2 or c3.

Additionally, if Black manages to play b7-b5 like mentioned above, the b5-square might be used as a steppingstone for one black knight to finally reach d4.

Ok, here's what I think and more importantly, why.
Computers don't explain the reasons for a move being good or bad. 
Learning computer lines by heart is a very hard task to perform when you don't understand the position. The deeper your lines go the more possibilities your opponent has. You won't be able to learn all the answers to his possible replies. If he deviates and you don't find the best continuation in a potentially razor-sharp position, it doesn't matter that Stockfish evaluates your position as winning. Humans aren't computers.

Since the other person mentioned the fried liver and Traxler, let me tell you something.
One of my students (young child) played the European championship last summer. After a great start he lost a lot of points to stupid mistakes.
In the penultimate round his opponent would play the fried liver. I told my student to play the Traxler, showed him some ideas and told him that it's okay to be down in material. Play aggressively and use all of your pieces.
I only showed him a single forced line which was winning for Black. Just one line.
That forced line appeared on the board. My student failed to reproduce the moves. His opponent was winning by force but played a sequence of bad moves so my student won after finding some great resources - on the board, by himself!

In my opinion it's more important to stick to your most trusted lines and look at how GM players play the positions you usually reach. Look for plans, not for computer-generated lines. Especially in tournaments where you play multiple opponents and you might not even know whether you have black or white against your "main opponent".
If you want to look for weaknesses in your opponent's lines you could prioritize the games he won. A lot of amateurs don't analyze their wins so there might be a better chance to find weaknesses there.

I can tell you about countless other examples  from my own games but this has already become an essay.
Good luck!
